prompt: What is the limiting reagent in a chemical reaction?

choices.text: The reactant that runs out first, which stops the reaction
The reactant that is left over when the reaction stops
choices.why: A reactant that is left over is in excess. The limiting reagent is the one you run out of.

choices.text: The reactant present in the smallest mass at the start
choices.why: The smallest mass isn't necessarily the first to run out; that depends on moles and on the balanced equation.

choices.text: The product that forms in the smallest amount
choices.why: The limiting reagent is a reactant, not a product. It is the reactant that gives the least amount of product.

explanation: You usually run out of one reactant before all of the others have reacted. The reactant you run out of is the limiting reagent; the other reactants are in excess.

prompt: In a chemical reaction, what does it mean to say that a reactant is in excess?

choices.text: Some of it remains after the reaction is complete.
It is used up before any other reactant.
choices.why: The reactant that is used up first is the limiting reagent, not the one in excess.

choices.text: Its starting mass is larger than that of any other reactant.
choices.why: Mass alone doesn't decide it. A reactant with a smaller mass can still be in excess, depending on its moles and the balanced equation.

choices.text: It has the largest coefficient in the balanced equation.
choices.why: Coefficients give the ratio in which substances react. Whether a reactant is in excess depends on how much of each is actually present.

explanation: When the limiting reagent runs out, the reaction stops. Any other reactant still has some left over, so it is said to be in excess.

prompt: To identify the limiting reagent, you calculate how much of one product each reactant could make. What do you assume about the reactant in each of those calculations?

choices.text: All of that reactant reacts.
That reactant is in excess.
choices.why: A reactant in excess has some left over. Each calculation instead assumes that all of the reactant reacts, so none of it is left.

choices.text: The reactants are present in equal masses.
choices.why: You use the actual starting amount of each reactant, whatever it is. The masses don't need to be equal.

choices.text: The other reactant runs out first.
choices.why: If the other reactant ran out first, not all of this one could react. Each calculation imagines its own reactant reacting completely.

explanation: Each calculation assumes that all of that reactant reacts. Comparing the results shows which reactant would give the lesser amount of product, and that reactant is the limiting reagent.

prompt: Two students find the limiting reagent for the same reaction mixture. Both calculate how much CO2 each reactant could make, but one works in moles of CO2 and the other in grams of CO2. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Both students will identify the same limiting reagent.
Only the student working in moles is correct, because equations are balanced in moles.
choices.why: Both students use moles to go through the balanced equation. Converting each result to grams of CO2 just multiplies both by the same molar mass, so the smaller result stays smaller.

choices.text: Only the student working in grams is correct, because the reactants were weighed in grams.
choices.why: How the reactants were measured doesn't matter here. Moles or grams of the product both work for the comparison.

choices.text: The students may identify different limiting reagents, so neither result can be trusted.
choices.why: Both results for each reactant are multiplied by the same molar mass of CO2, so the order of the two amounts can't change.

explanation: It does not matter whether you determine moles or grams of the product. Converting moles of CO2 to grams multiplies both results by the same molar mass, so the reactant that gives the lesser amount in moles also gives the lesser amount in grams.

prompt: Hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms are being combined to make water molecules, H2O. The oxygen atoms run out while some hydrogen atoms are still left. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Oxygen is the limiting reagent, and no more water molecules can form.
Hydrogen is the limiting reagent, because some of it is left over.
choices.why: The reactant that is left over is in excess. The limiting reagent is the one you run out of, which here is oxygen.

choices.text: Oxygen is the limiting reagent, but the leftover hydrogen keeps forming water.
choices.why: Every water molecule needs an oxygen atom. With no oxygen atoms left, no more water molecules can be made.

choices.text: Oxygen is in excess, because all of it was used up.
choices.why: In excess means some is left over. Oxygen was used up completely, so it is the limiting reagent and hydrogen is in excess.

explanation: The reactant you run out of is the limiting reagent, so oxygen limits here and hydrogen is in excess. Every water molecule needs an oxygen atom, so the process stops when the oxygen atoms run out.

prompt: Nitrogen and hydrogen react according to N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. A mixture contains 1.50 mol N2 and 4.50 mol H2. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Both reactants run out at the same time, so neither is left over.
N2 is the limiting reagent, because fewer moles of it are present.
choices.why: Comparing moles of reactants ignores the coefficients. Each reactant could make 3.00 mol NH3, so they run out together.

choices.text: H2 is the limiting reagent, because 3 mol of it is needed for each 1 mol of N2.
choices.why: 4.50 mol H2 is exactly 3 times 1.50 mol N2, which is just enough to react with all of the N2.

choices.text: H2 is in excess, because more moles of it are present.
choices.why: 4.50 mol H2 reacts completely with 1.50 mol N2, so none of the H2 is left over.

explanation: 1.50 mol N2 × (2 mol NH3 / 1 mol N2) = 3.00 mol NH3, and 4.50 mol H2 × (2 mol NH3 / 3 mol H2) = 3.00 mol NH3. The reactants are present in the proper quantities, so both are used up together.

prompt: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid according to Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. In one experiment, Zn is the limiting reagent and HCl is in excess. The experiment is repeated with the same mass of Zn but twice as much HCl. How does the mass of H2 formed compare with the first experiment?

choices.text: The same, because the Zn still runs out at the same point
Twice as great, because twice as much HCl is present
choices.why: Adding more of a reactant that is already in excess doesn't make more product. The amount of the limiting reagent, Zn, sets how much H2 forms.

choices.text: Greater, because the reaction now uses up all of the HCl
choices.why: Some HCl was already left over in the first experiment. With more HCl added, even more of it is left over.

choices.text: Less, because HCl now becomes the limiting reagent
choices.why: Adding more of a reactant can't make it run out sooner. HCl is still in excess, and Zn is still the limiting reagent.

explanation: The limiting reagent decides how much product forms. Once the Zn is used up the reaction stops, so the extra HCl just adds to the amount left over and the same mass of H2 forms.

prompt: You have identified the limiting reagent in a reaction. How do you find the mass of the excess reagent that is left over?

choices.text: Calculate the mass of it that reacts with all of the limiting reagent, then subtract that from its starting mass.
Calculate the mass of it that reacts with all of the limiting reagent; that mass is the amount left over.
choices.why: That mass is the amount that reacted, not the amount remaining. You still have to subtract it from the starting mass.

choices.text: Subtract the starting mass of the limiting reagent from the starting mass of the excess reagent.
choices.why: Reactants don't react gram for gram. A mass-mass calculation using the balanced equation is needed to find how much excess reagent reacted.

choices.text: Subtract the mass of product formed from the starting mass of the excess reagent.
choices.why: The product contains atoms from the limiting reagent too, so its mass doesn't tell you how much of the excess reagent reacted.

explanation: A mass-mass calculation from the limiting reagent to the other reagent gives the mass that reacted, which you subtract from the original amount. A common error is to report the mass that reacted as the amount remaining.

prompt: A balanced chemical equation is like a recipe. A pancake recipe calls for 2 cups of pancake mix, 1 egg, and 1/2 cup of milk to make 1 batch. If you have 5 cups of mix, 3 eggs, and 4 cups of milk, which ingredient acts as the limiting reagent?

choices.text: The pancake mix, which is enough for only 2.5 batches
The eggs, because 3 is the smallest amount on hand
choices.why: Amounts of different ingredients can't be compared directly; the recipe has to be used. 3 eggs at 1 egg per batch is enough for 3 batches, more than the mix allows.

choices.text: The milk, which is enough for only 2 batches
choices.why: Each batch needs only 1/2 cup of milk, so 4 cups is enough for 8 batches. Dividing 4 cups by 2 instead of by 1/2 gives 2.

choices.text: No single ingredient, since they all run out together
choices.why: They run out at different points: the mix after 2.5 batches, the eggs after 3, and the milk after 8.

explanation: Find how many batches each ingredient allows: 5 cups ÷ 2 cups per batch = 2.5 batches of mix, 3 eggs ÷ 1 egg per batch = 3 batches, and 4 cups ÷ 1/2 cup per batch = 8 batches of milk. The mix runs out first, so it limits; the eggs and milk are in excess.

prompt: Sulfur dioxide reacts with oxygen according to 2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3. If 3.0 mol SO2 and 2.0 mol O2 are mixed, which reactant is the limiting reagent, and why?

choices.text: SO2, because it can make only 3.0 mol SO3, while the O2 could make 4.0 mol
O2, because it can make 4.0 mol SO3, while the SO2 could make only 3.0 mol
choices.why: The limiting reagent is the reactant that gives the lesser amount of product, not the greater.

choices.text: O2, because fewer moles of O2 are present than of SO2
choices.why: Comparing moles of the reactants ignores the coefficients. Using up 2.0 mol O2 would take 4.0 mol SO2, more than is present.

choices.text: Neither, because both reactants will be used up completely
choices.why: Using up all 2.0 mol O2 would take 4.0 mol SO2, but only 3.0 mol is present, so SO2 runs out first and some O2 is left over.

explanation: 3.0 mol SO2 × (2 mol SO3 / 2 mol SO2) = 3.0 mol SO3, and 2.0 mol O2 × (2 mol SO3 / 1 mol O2) = 4.0 mol SO3. SO2 gives the lesser amount, so it is the limiting reagent even though more moles of it are present.

prompt: Sodium reacts with chlorine according to 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl. A reaction starts with 10.0 g of Na (molar mass 22.99 g/mol) and 10.0 g of Cl2 (molar mass 70.90 g/mol). Which reactant is the limiting reagent, and why?

choices.text: Cl2, because it can make only 0.282 mol NaCl, while the Na could make 0.435 mol
Na, because it can make 0.435 mol NaCl, while the Cl2 could make only 0.282 mol
choices.why: The limiting reagent is the reactant that gives the lesser amount of product, not the greater.

choices.text: Na, because the equation needs 2 mol of Na for every 1 mol of Cl2
choices.why: The coefficients alone don't decide it. 10.0 g Na is 0.435 mol, which needs only 0.217 mol Cl2, but 10.0 g Cl2 is just 0.141 mol, so Cl2 runs out first.

choices.text: Neither, because equal masses of the two reactants are present
choices.why: Equal masses are not equal numbers of moles. Cl2 has a much larger molar mass, so 10.0 g of it is fewer moles, and it runs out first.

explanation: 10.0 g Na × (1 mol Na / 22.99 g Na) × (2 mol NaCl / 2 mol Na) = 0.435 mol NaCl, and 10.0 g Cl2 × (1 mol Cl2 / 70.90 g Cl2) × (2 mol NaCl / 1 mol Cl2) = 0.282 mol NaCl. Cl2 gives the lesser amount, so it is the limiting reagent and Na is in excess.

prompt: Iron(III) oxide reacts with carbon monoxide according to Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. A mixture contains 100.0 g of Fe2O3 (molar mass 159.70 g/mol) and 60.0 g of CO (molar mass 28.01 g/mol). Which is the limiting reagent, and how many moles of Fe form?

choices.text: Fe2O3 is limiting, and 1.25 mol Fe forms
CO is limiting, and 1.43 mol Fe forms
choices.why: CO could make 1.43 mol Fe, more than the 1.25 mol from the Fe2O3. Having the smaller mass doesn't make CO the limiting reagent; giving the lesser amount of product does.

choices.text: Fe2O3 is limiting, and 0.626 mol Fe forms
choices.why: 0.626 mol is the amount of Fe2O3. Each mole of Fe2O3 makes 2 mol Fe, so 1.25 mol Fe forms.

choices.text: Neither is limiting, and 2.68 mol Fe forms
choices.why: The two amounts can't be added. The reaction stops when the Fe2O3 runs out, so only 1.25 mol Fe forms and some CO is left over.

explanation: 100.0 g Fe2O3 × (1 mol Fe2O3 / 159.70 g Fe2O3) × (2 mol Fe / 1 mol Fe2O3) = 1.25 mol Fe, and 60.0 g CO × (1 mol CO / 28.01 g CO) × (2 mol Fe / 3 mol CO) = 1.43 mol Fe. Fe2O3 gives the lesser amount, so it is the limiting reagent and 1.25 mol Fe forms.

prompt: Ethane burns according to 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O. For a mixture of 1.00 mol C2H6 and 3.00 mol O2, a student calculates that the C2H6 could make 2.00 mol CO2 and the O2 could make 2.57 mol H2O, and concludes that C2H6 is the limiting reagent. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The student compared two different products; compared on one product, O2 is the limiting reagent.
The student is correct, because 2.00 mol is less than 2.57 mol.
choices.why: Those are amounts of two different products, so they can't be compared. Using CO2 for both, the O2 gives only 1.71 mol, less than 2.00 mol.

choices.text: The student is correct, because fewer moles of C2H6 are present than of O2.
choices.why: Comparing moles of reactants ignores the coefficients. 1.00 mol C2H6 needs 3.50 mol O2, more than the 3.00 mol present.

choices.text: The student compared two different products; compared on one product, neither reactant is limiting.
choices.why: On one product the amounts are not equal: for CO2 they are 2.00 mol and 1.71 mol. The O2 gives the lesser amount, so it is the limiting reagent.

explanation: It doesn't matter which product you use, but it must be the same one for each reactant. Using CO2, 1.00 mol C2H6 × (4 mol CO2 / 2 mol C2H6) = 2.00 mol CO2 and 3.00 mol O2 × (4 mol CO2 / 7 mol O2) = 1.71 mol CO2, so O2 gives the lesser amount and is the limiting reagent.

prompt: Two reactants, A and B, react to form a single product. If all of A reacted, it would make 0.48 mol of product; if all of B reacted, it would make 0.62 mol. How many moles of product actually form when the reaction is complete?
explanation: The reactant that gives the lesser amount of product is the limiting reagent. A runs out after 0.48 mol of product has formed, so the reaction stops there and some B is left over.

prompt: Water molecules, H2O, are built from separate hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms. If you start with 6 hydrogen atoms and 5 oxygen atoms and make as many water molecules as possible, how many oxygen atoms are left over?
explanation: Each H2O needs 2 H atoms and 1 O atom. The 6 H atoms are enough for only 3 molecules, while the 5 O atoms would be enough for 5, so hydrogen runs out first. The 3 molecules use 3 O atoms, leaving 5 − 3 = 2.

prompt: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. What is the greatest number of NH3 molecules that can form from 10 N2 molecules and 24 H2 molecules?
explanation: 10 molecules N2 × (2 molecules NH3 / 1 molecule N2) = 20 molecules NH3, and 24 molecules H2 × (2 molecules NH3 / 3 molecules H2) = 16 molecules NH3. H2 gives the lesser amount, so it is the limiting reagent and 16 NH3 molecules form.

prompt: Propane burns according to C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. How many moles of H2O form from a mixture of 0.500 mol C3H8 and 2.00 mol O2?
explanation: 0.500 mol C3H8 × (4 mol H2O / 1 mol C3H8) = 2.00 mol H2O, and 2.00 mol O2 × (4 mol H2O / 5 mol O2) = 1.60 mol H2O. O2 is the limiting reagent even though more moles of it are present, so 1.60 mol H2O forms.

prompt: Carbon monoxide burns according to 2CO + O2 → 2CO2, and all three substances are gases. A sealed container holds 4.00 mol CO and 3.00 mol O2, which react until one of them is used up. How many moles of gas, in total, are in the container afterward?
explanation: 4.00 mol CO can make 4.00 mol CO2, while 3.00 mol O2 could make 6.00 mol, so CO is the limiting reagent. The 4.00 mol CO uses 2.00 mol O2, leaving 1.00 mol O2, so the container holds 4.00 mol CO2 + 1.00 mol O2 = 5.00 mol of gas.

prompt: Aluminum reacts with oxygen according to 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3. What mass of Al2O3 (molar mass 101.96 g/mol), in grams, forms from 5.00 mol Al and 4.50 mol O2?
explanation: 5.00 mol Al × (2 mol Al2O3 / 4 mol Al) = 2.50 mol Al2O3, and 4.50 mol O2 × (2 mol Al2O3 / 3 mol O2) = 3.00 mol Al2O3, so Al is the limiting reagent. 2.50 mol Al2O3 × (101.96 g Al2O3 / 1 mol Al2O3) = 254.9 g Al2O3.

prompt: Carbon disulfide burns according to CS2 + 3O2 → CO2 + 2SO2. How many moles of SO2 form from 10.0 g of CS2 (molar mass 76.13 g/mol) and 20.0 g of O2 (molar mass 32.00 g/mol)?
explanation: 10.0 g CS2 × (1 mol CS2 / 76.13 g CS2) × (2 mol SO2 / 1 mol CS2) = 0.263 mol SO2, and 20.0 g O2 × (1 mol O2 / 32.00 g O2) × (2 mol SO2 / 3 mol O2) = 0.417 mol SO2. CS2 gives the lesser amount, so it is the limiting reagent and 0.263 mol SO2 forms.

prompt: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid according to Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. What mass of H2, in grams, forms from 6.00 g of Mg and 15.0 g of HCl? Use molar masses of 24.31 g/mol for Mg, 36.46 g/mol for HCl, and 2.016 g/mol for H2.
explanation: 6.00 g Mg × (1 mol Mg / 24.31 g Mg) × (1 mol H2 / 1 mol Mg) = 0.247 mol H2, and 15.0 g HCl × (1 mol HCl / 36.46 g HCl) × (1 mol H2 / 2 mol HCl) = 0.206 mol H2, so HCl is the limiting reagent. 0.206 mol H2 × (2.016 g H2 / 1 mol H2) = 0.415 g H2.

prompt: Hydrogen burns in oxygen according to 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. What mass of H2O, in grams, forms from 10.0 g of H2 and 64.0 g of O2? Use molar masses of 2.016 g/mol for H2, 32.00 g/mol for O2, and 18.02 g/mol for H2O.
explanation: 10.0 g H2 × (1 mol H2 / 2.016 g H2) × (2 mol H2O / 2 mol H2) = 4.96 mol H2O, and 64.0 g O2 × (1 mol O2 / 32.00 g O2) × (2 mol H2O / 1 mol O2) = 4.00 mol H2O, so O2 is the limiting reagent even though the H2 has the smaller mass. 4.00 mol H2O × (18.02 g H2O / 1 mol H2O) = 72.1 g H2O.

prompt: Silver nitrate and sodium chloride react to form a precipitate: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq). What mass of AgCl, in grams, forms from 8.50 g of AgNO3 and 2.00 g of NaCl? Use molar masses of 169.88 g/mol for AgNO3, 58.44 g/mol for NaCl, and 143.32 g/mol for AgCl.
explanation: 8.50 g AgNO3 × (1 mol AgNO3 / 169.88 g AgNO3) × (1 mol AgCl / 1 mol AgNO3) = 0.0500 mol AgCl, and 2.00 g NaCl × (1 mol NaCl / 58.44 g NaCl) × (1 mol AgCl / 1 mol NaCl) = 0.0342 mol AgCl, so NaCl is the limiting reagent. 0.0342 mol AgCl × (143.32 g AgCl / 1 mol AgCl) = 4.90 g AgCl.

prompt: Baking soda (NaHCO3) reacts with the acetic acid (HC2H3O2) in vinegar according to NaHCO3 + HC2H3O2 → NaC2H3O2 + H2O + CO2. What mass of CO2, in grams, can form from 5.00 g of NaHCO3 and 3.00 g of HC2H3O2? Use molar masses of 84.01 g/mol for NaHCO3, 60.05 g/mol for HC2H3O2, and 44.01 g/mol for CO2.
explanation: 5.00 g NaHCO3 × (1 mol NaHCO3 / 84.01 g NaHCO3) × (1 mol CO2 / 1 mol NaHCO3) = 0.0595 mol CO2, and 3.00 g HC2H3O2 × (1 mol HC2H3O2 / 60.05 g HC2H3O2) × (1 mol CO2 / 1 mol HC2H3O2) = 0.0500 mol CO2, so the acetic acid is the limiting reagent. 0.0500 mol CO2 × (44.01 g CO2 / 1 mol CO2) = 2.20 g CO2.

prompt: Magnesium burns in oxygen according to 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. A student reacts 4.86 g of Mg with 4.00 g of O2 and collects 7.25 g of MgO. What is the percent yield? Use molar masses of 24.31 g/mol for Mg, 32.00 g/mol for O2, and 40.31 g/mol for MgO.
explanation: 4.86 g Mg × (1 mol Mg / 24.31 g Mg) × (2 mol MgO / 2 mol Mg) = 0.200 mol MgO, and 4.00 g O2 × (1 mol O2 / 32.00 g O2) × (2 mol MgO / 1 mol O2) = 0.250 mol MgO, so Mg is the limiting reagent. The theoretical yield is 0.200 mol × 40.31 g/mol = 8.06 g MgO, so the percent yield is (7.25 g / 8.06 g) × 100% = 90.0%.

prompt: Methane burns according to CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. A mixture of 2.00 mol CH4 and 5.00 mol O2 reacts until one reactant is used up. How many moles of the excess reagent are left over?
explanation: 2.00 mol CH4 × (1 mol CO2 / 1 mol CH4) = 2.00 mol CO2, while 5.00 mol O2 × (1 mol CO2 / 2 mol O2) = 2.50 mol CO2, so CH4 is the limiting reagent and O2 is in excess. 2.00 mol CH4 × (2 mol O2 / 1 mol CH4) = 4.00 mol O2 reacts, leaving 5.00 mol − 4.00 mol = 1.00 mol O2.

prompt: Aluminum reacts with chlorine according to 2Al + 3Cl2 → 2AlCl3. A mixture contains 0.600 mol Al and 0.600 mol Cl2. What mass of the excess reagent, in grams, is left over when the reaction is complete? The molar mass of Al is 26.98 g/mol, and that of Cl2 is 70.90 g/mol.
explanation: 0.600 mol Al × (2 mol AlCl3 / 2 mol Al) = 0.600 mol AlCl3, and 0.600 mol Cl2 × (2 mol AlCl3 / 3 mol Cl2) = 0.400 mol AlCl3, so Cl2 is the limiting reagent. It reacts with 0.600 mol Cl2 × (2 mol Al / 3 mol Cl2) = 0.400 mol Al, leaving 0.200 mol Al × 26.98 g/mol = 5.40 g Al.

prompt: Iron reacts with oxygen according to 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. A reaction starts with 30.0 g of Fe (molar mass 55.85 g/mol) and 10.0 g of O2 (molar mass 32.00 g/mol). What mass of the excess reagent, in grams, remains after the reaction is complete?
explanation: 30.0 g Fe × (1 mol Fe / 55.85 g Fe) × (2 mol Fe2O3 / 4 mol Fe) = 0.269 mol Fe2O3, and 10.0 g O2 × (1 mol O2 / 32.00 g O2) × (2 mol Fe2O3 / 3 mol O2) = 0.208 mol Fe2O3, so O2 is limiting and Fe is in excess. 10.0 g O2 × (1 mol O2 / 32.00 g O2) × (4 mol Fe / 3 mol O2) × (55.85 g Fe / 1 mol Fe) = 23.27 g Fe reacts, leaving 30.0 g − 23.27 g = 6.73 g Fe.

prompt: Zinc and sulfur react according to Zn + S → ZnS. A student heats 10.0 g of Zn (molar mass 65.39 g/mol) with 8.00 g of S (molar mass 32.06 g/mol) and predicts that the sulfur will be used up because there is less of it. What mass of sulfur, in grams, is actually left over?
explanation: 10.0 g Zn × (1 mol Zn / 65.39 g Zn) = 0.153 mol Zn, which can make 0.153 mol ZnS, while 8.00 g S × (1 mol S / 32.06 g S) = 0.250 mol S could make 0.250 mol ZnS, so Zn is the limiting reagent. The Zn reacts with 0.153 mol S × 32.06 g/mol = 4.90 g S, leaving 8.00 g − 4.90 g = 3.10 g S.

prompt: Copper reacts with silver nitrate according to Cu + 2AgNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag. A 5.00 g piece of copper wire (molar mass of Cu 63.55 g/mol) is placed in a solution containing 10.0 g of AgNO3 (molar mass 169.88 g/mol). When the reaction is complete, what mass of copper, in grams, remains?
explanation: 5.00 g Cu × (1 mol Cu / 63.55 g Cu) × (2 mol Ag / 1 mol Cu) = 0.157 mol Ag, and 10.0 g AgNO3 × (1 mol AgNO3 / 169.88 g AgNO3) × (2 mol Ag / 2 mol AgNO3) = 0.0589 mol Ag, so AgNO3 is the limiting reagent. 10.0 g AgNO3 × (1 mol AgNO3 / 169.88 g AgNO3) × (1 mol Cu / 2 mol AgNO3) × (63.55 g Cu / 1 mol Cu) = 1.87 g Cu reacts, leaving 5.00 g − 1.87 g = 3.13 g Cu.
